newsitem.title: EGYPT: Europe says will act with U.S. for Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: Europe says will act with U.S. for Mideast peace.

text.p: Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said on Monday Europe, frustrated at being cut out of the U.S.-brokered Middle East peace process, would work with Washington, not against it, to galvanise the peace talks.

"There is no competition between Europeans and Americans. We want to work together, we both have roles to play in this very important process and we are going to work together in that respect," Spring told reporters at this northeastern town after meeting Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.
Although the United States co-sponsored a 1991 peace conference in Madrid, its role in the region has traditionally been seen as tilted towards Israel.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat stopped in both France and Italy on his way home last week from an emergency meeting with Netanyahu in Washington to ask for a European presence in talks with the Jewish state.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said Spring, sent by the European Union to meet Israeli and Palestinian officials, confirmed the anxiety of the 15-nation bloc about the stalemate and its offer to help with negotiations.
Ireland currently holds the rotating EU presidency.

"We have reaffirmed our desire to offer assistance to the peace process and also our desire that concise and concrete steps are taken (by Palestinians and Israelis) to show the world that the peace process is on the right track," Spring told reporters earlier in Cairo.
"Europe is very worried at not having a force in the region to push the peace process...We are watching the situation closely," he added.
Spring also said Europe was also willing to offer financial and political help to support Palestinian-Israeli peace accords and that it would appoint a special envoy to the region.
Spring will set off for Israel later on Monday for a potentially controversial trip to Israel and Gaza.
Irish minister has said he may meet Palestinian officials in Orient House, their offices in disputed Arab East Jerusalem.

Israel has strongly condemned the venue, adding it may even refuse to meet Spring if he visited the offices, seen by Israel as backing for Palestinian claims to East Jerusalem which the Jewish state occupied in 1967.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher left Israel earlier on Monday after two-days of pressuring Israel into honouring a promised troop withdrawal from Hebron, the last of seven towns to be given Palestinian autonomy.

Israeli and Palestinian negotiatiors also met on Monday to discuss the long delayed troop pull-back and other peace pledges put on hold since hardline Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was elected in May.

Netanyahu, who angered the Palestinians, Arabs and Europe by saying he wanted to alter a 1993 peace deal to secure Jewish settlers living in Hebron, told parliament on Monday he would stick to the troop withdrawal as stipulated by the accord.
But he did not give a date or details of the security arrangements his negotiators were wrangling out with the Palestinians.
Moussa said Egypt, host of several rounds of peace negotiations, also welcomed the EU's involvement as "additional support" to the American and Egyptian role.

"This will support the American and Egyptian involvement in the peace process, particularly as the European role is known for its clarity and a position based on the (1991) Madrid and (1993) Oslo peace accords," the Egyptian minister added.
